title: I got tired of using 10 different apps to understand the market, so I built one
author: Square-Historian1458

comments.author: Beginning_Support_86
comments.body:
one piece of feedback that is cheap now and impossible to retrofit later: whatever the Decision Radar outputs, write it to an append-only log with a timestamp, and make that history public.



right now Watch / Wait / Avoid is unfalsifiable. if the current call is all anyone can see, then nobody can ever tell whether it works, and that includes you. six months of timestamped calls is the only thing that turns it from a feature into evidence, and it costs you almost nothing today versus reconstructing it later from data you did not keep.



the same applies to the regime flag. risk-on / risk-off classifiers are easy to build and almost always backward looking, and the honest question is what the label predicted rather than what it described. you cannot answer that without the archive either.



separate and worth checking early: "Avoid" attached to a named asset for retail users is closer to a recommendation than to information in a lot of jurisdictions, and the exposure does not depend on whether you charge for it. plenty of dashboards get around this by surfacing the inputs and letting the user draw the conclusion. worth a look before it is load bearing in your marketing.

replies.author: Square-Historian1458
replies.body:
Thanks, this is genuinely valuable feedback.

I like the idea of a public timestamped archive. I already keep the lifecycle of scenarios internally (new - confirmed - closed), but making that history public would make Pulse much more transparent.

Good point on the regulatory side too. The goal is to provide context, not trading recommendations, so I'll definitely rethink how those labels are presented.

Really appreciate you taking the time to write this

replies.author: Beginning_Support_86
replies.body:
that lifecycle log means most of the work is already done, so the gap is smaller than it looks. two details decide whether it ends up being worth anything though.



make it append-only rather than a status field. new / confirmed / closed as a column that gets updated in place records the current state, but what you need is the history of transitions with the time each one was written. otherwise the record cannot distinguish a call that was right from a call that was quietly amended, and that stays true even for you reading your own data six months from now. same row count, completely different evidential value.



and publish the ones that never got confirmed. if the public archive only holds scenarios that reached confirmed or closed, it is a filtered set and it will look better than the system actually is. the ones that got flagged and then went nowhere are your control group, and they are the only thing that makes the confirmed ones mean anything.



on the labels, one thing to be careful about: rewording Avoid to something softer changes little if a user can still act on it directly without doing any analysis of their own. what actually changes the character is showing the inputs behind the call and letting them draw the conclusion. that is also the better product, because the people who will pay for this are the ones who want to see the reasoning.

replies.author: Square-Historian1458
replies.body:
That's a really good point.

I hadn't thought about the difference between storing the current state and storing the actual transition history, but you're right-that's what makes it auditable instead of just historical.

I also agree about keeping the "failed" scenarios in the archive. Without them, any success rate would be misleading.

And yes, the reasoning is ultimately more valuable than the label itself. The long-term goal is for users to see why  Pulse reached a conclusion, not just the conclusion.

Thanks again for taking the time to write this. This is exactly the kind of feedback I was hoping for.
